opus-5.5.text:
That was really my first serious paper, from my early PhD days at UC San Diego working with Zhuowen Tu, together with Chen-Yu Lee. Looking back, I'd say its value lies less in the specific method and more in the question it was asking at the time.

Around 2014, people were just starting to train deeper networks after AlexNet, and training was genuinely hard. Gradients vanished, optimization was unstable, and the intermediate layers didn't necessarily learn discriminative features. Our idea was simple: why only supervise the final output? We attached auxiliary classifiers to the hidden layers, adding a "companion" loss at each stage, so every layer receives a more direct signal about what it should learn. That made the training more stable, the features more discriminative, and it acted as a kind of regularization.

In the longer arc, I think deep supervision was one of several attempts at the same underlying problem: how do you make very deep networks trainable? GoogLeNet used auxiliary classifiers in a similar spirit around the same time. Then ResNet came along, and skip connections addressed the optimization problem far more elegantly and at the architecture level. So in a sense, the problem DSN was patching got solved more fundamentally, and the field moved on. I think that's healthy. Many papers are stepping stones rather than endpoints.

But the idea itself didn't disappear. It lives on in a lot of places. In dense prediction tasks like edge detection, our follow-up work HED, Holistically-Nested Edge Detection, used deep supervision on side outputs, and that worked very well because multi-scale intermediate features really matter there. You see it in segmentation networks, in medical imaging, in various multi-scale designs. More broadly, the question of "what should intermediate representations learn, and how do we give them signals?" is still alive, whether through representation alignment, intermediate losses in generative models, or probing what different layers of large models encode.

On a personal level, it taught me something important: a simple idea that's clearly motivated can have a long life, even if its original justification gets superseded. And it shaped my taste. I've always cared about representations and architectures, about what happens inside the network, not just the final number. That interest started with DSN.

r001.rationale: The response says deep supervision and ResNet address the same underlying problem of making very deep networks trainable.

r002.rationale: It describes deep supervision continuing in later work, including the speaker’s HED follow-up, but does not say researchers unknowingly reused designs from their own earlier work years later.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, Deeply Supervised Nets feels like a very early piece of work, but it also feels like a seed for a lot of what came after, both for me personally and for the field.

The context matters. This was 2014. AlexNet had just happened, and everyone was realizing that depth was the thing, but we didn't yet understand how to train deep networks reliably. Gradients would vanish, optimization would stall, and there was this real sense that the deeper you went, the more fragile things became. Batch normalization hadn't come out yet, residual connections hadn't come out yet. So the question we were asking was very simple: if the problem is that the signal from the loss gets weaker the further it has to travel back, why not just put supervision closer to the intermediate layers?

That idea, adding companion objectives to hidden layers, was almost naive in a way. But it worked, and more importantly it reflected a way of thinking that I've carried with me since. You look at where the learning signal is and ask how to make it more direct. GoogLeNet did something similar with auxiliary classifiers around the same time, which told us we were touching on something real.

In the longer arc, I'd say two things. First, the specific technique got largely subsumed. Once ResNets arrived, you had a cleaner architectural solution to the same optimization problem, and deep supervision as a training trick became less necessary for standard classification. So in a narrow sense, it's a method that was overtaken.

But second, and this is the part I find more interesting, the underlying idea never really went away. It kept resurfacing in different clothes. In segmentation and detection you see intermediate predictions at multiple scales. In holistically nested edge detection, which I worked on right after with Zhuowen Tu, deep supervision was central. In some ways even the later discussions about where representations form inside a network, and how you probe or train intermediate layers, come from a similar intuition.

So I don't think of it as a landmark result. I think of it as an honest attempt to understand an optimization problem with the tools we had at the time, and as the moment I learned that studying how a network trains is as important as what architecture you draw. That mindset of asking why something is hard to optimize, rather than just scaling past it, has stayed with me through ResNeXt, through ConvNeXt, and into the work I do now. It also gave me a lot of appreciation for how fast ideas become obsolete, and how what survives is usually the question rather than the method.

r001.rationale: The response says Deeply Supervised Nets addressed the difficulty of optimizing deep networks and that ResNets later provided a cleaner architectural solution to the same optimization problem.

r002.rationale: The response says the underlying idea resurfaced and that its own mindset persisted, but does not observe that researchers may unknowingly reuse designs from their own earlier work years later.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to separate the specific method from the question behind it. Deeply Supervised Nets asks: why should the learning signal come only at the end of a network? What happens if we also supervise intermediate representations?

In the longer course of research, a particular technique may become less necessary as architectures and optimization methods change. But the underlying question can remain useful. Here, that question is how to help different parts of a deep model learn meaningful representations.

So I wouldn’t judge its significance only by whether people still use the exact formulation. I’d also ask whether it gave us a useful way to think about training deep networks. Research often moves forward that way: the implementation changes, but a question continues to inform what comes next.

sol-6.1.text:
I see Deeply Supervised Nets as an early exploration of a question that is still relevant: where should the learning signal enter a network? Instead of putting supervision only at the final output, you also give intermediate representations a more direct training signal.

At the time, that was useful for thinking about optimization and how features develop across layers. As architectures and training methods improved, some of the original motivation became less pressing. But the broader idea—that intermediate representations can benefit from explicit objectives—has continued to be useful.

So I would view it as one step in a longer conversation, rather than a recipe that every network should follow. The lasting question is when additional supervision helps a representation, and when it constrains it too much.
